video_title: Liz Truss: The Right Has to Dismantle Blair’s State
gist: Former UK prime minister Liz Truss tells Peter McCormack the UK is in accelerating decline driven by Keynesian money printing, an unaccountable Bank of England, OBR/Treasury short-termism and Blair-era technocratic institutions, and that no right-wing party yet commits to making the Bank of England accountable. She sees a 2029 election risk of another Labour-led government, a possible euro-area/France crisis first, and frames Bitcoin as a bulwark against centralized state power.

themes.theme: UK fiscal decline and debt arithmetic

insights.claim: Liz Truss argues the UK has not generated a budget surplus for 30 years, living standards have fallen relative to the US over that period, and Britain is being overtaken by Poland and Slovenia on living standards.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Structural UK underperformance thesis supports a bearish long-term stance on sterling/gilts relative to US assets.
insights.quote: the country hasn't generated a surplus for 30 years

insights.claim: Peter McCormack cites UK public borrowing of about 24.5 billion pounds in a recent month, of which about 11 billion was debt interest, and roughly 60% of last-quarter borrowing funded day-to-day government spending rather than investment.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack
insights.so_what: Debt interest consuming close to half of monthly borrowing signals rising gilt-supply and fiscal-dominance risk.

insights.claim: Truss says the Office for Budget Responsibility, created in 2010 to deliver fiscal discipline, has instead coincided with UK debt reaching about 3 trillion pounds.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Markets should not treat OBR-based fiscal rules as a credible anchor for UK debt sustainability.
insights.quote: it's not led to fiscal discipline it's led to a3 trillion pound debt

insights.claim: Truss explains that 'fiscal headroom' means debt is forecast to start falling in five years if OBR forecasts prove right, not spare money available today, and the forecast fall is perpetually pushed out.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Treat headroom announcements around UK budgets skeptically; small forecast misses force tax rises or cuts that move gilts.

insights.claim: Truss and McCormack cite IEA research finding the UK is poorer per capita than Mississippi, the poorest US state, while the public believed it was as rich as the seventh-richest state.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Public underestimation of UK relative poverty implies delayed political appetite for reform, prolonging decline.
insights.quote: we're poorer than Mississippi, the poorest US state

insights.claim: Truss reports a record rate of billionaires leaving the UK and says millions of people want to leave Britain, which she expects a wealth tax to accelerate.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Capital and talent flight erodes the UK tax base; watch wealth-tax proposals as a trigger for further outflows.

insights.claim: McCormack argues that a growing share of UK voters work for the state, work in heavily regulated captured industries such as banks and energy, or receive benefits, leaving a shrinking group propping up the economy and little electoral incentive for reform.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack
insights.so_what: Electoral arithmetic favors continued spending growth, implying persistent deficits and stealth tax rises.

insights.claim: McCormack says a recent UK budget contained a stealth tax rise forcing businesses to report taxes more frequently to improve government cash flow, raising accounting costs; he spends about a day a week on state-required administration.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack
insights.so_what: Rising compliance costs squeeze UK SME margins; a negative for domestically focused small-cap earnings.

themes.theme: Money printing, inflation and the Bank of England

insights.claim: Truss claims the Bank of England dropped the money supply from its inflation models in the 1990s, keeps printing money while inflation rises, and refuses to acknowledge the link, reflecting Keynesian dominance at the BoE and the Federal Reserve.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Expect central banks to under-react to monetary drivers of inflation; supports inflation hedges such as Bitcoin, gold and real assets.
insights.quote: The Bank of England took the money supply out of their equations to calculate inflation

insights.claim: Truss says the US midterm result was driven by cost of living, partly the Iran war but largely money printing, excessive debt and rampant inflation, the same dynamic as in Britain.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Inflation is a live political vulnerability in both the US and UK, raising odds of policy shifts on spending and Fed oversight.

insights.claim: Truss argues quantitative easing and quantitative tightening are barely discussed publicly despite their large impact on the economy and asset prices, and that QE has benefited asset holders at the expense of non-asset holders.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Track BoE QT pace closely as an underappreciated driver of gilt yields and asset prices.
insights.quote: it's benefited asset holders at the expense of people that don't hold assets

insights.claim: McCormack notes the Bank of England says inflation will hit 5% next year, suspects the true rate is nearer 8-9%, and points out that 14 years of 5% inflation halves the value of money.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack
insights.so_what: Expect persistent UK inflation above target; cash and nominal gilts lose real value, favoring hard assets.
insights.quote: 14 years of 5% inflation, the value of your money cuts in half

insights.claim: Truss says the 1998 legislation making the Bank of England independent renders the governor effectively unsackable except for absconding from the country, leaving an unaccountable institution controlling money printing.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Political pressure to curb BoE independence is a tail risk to gilt credibility and sterling if adopted by a future government.

insights.claim: Truss's book Bank Job argues that if there is a central bank, elected people who can be hired and fired must make the ultimate decisions on the money supply, and that none of the UK right-wing parties has committed to making the Bank of England accountable.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: A right-wing pledge to end BoE independence would be a major market event; currently not on any party platform.
insights.quote: none of them have said that the Bank of England needs to be made accountable

insights.claim: Truss says that as prime minister she was 'taken down' by the Bank of England and others, which convinced her the system itself is broken.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Illustrates that the BoE and gilt market act as a hard constraint on UK fiscal policy shifts.

insights.claim: Truss supports Trump's push to take more control of the Federal Reserve as entirely reasonable and notes he faced massive pushback despite a huge mandate.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Fed independence remains a contested political issue; erosion would raise inflation-risk premia in Treasuries and the dollar.

insights.claim: Truss believes a crisis forcing monetary reform may come first in the euro area, possibly France, but complicit central banks printing money make a gradual-then-faster decline more likely than a sharp reset.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Watch French spreads (OAT-Bund) as the likely first crisis point in Europe; expect central bank backstops to delay resolution.
insights.quote: I think you're possibly going to see that with France

insights.claim: Truss argues the OBR and Treasury assess policy on a five-year horizon that is too short for tax changes; she wanted to keep corporation tax at 19% instead of raising it to 24% in 2022, but the OBR scored it as costing about 25 billion over five years, while independent economists at the CBR agreed it would pay for itself sooner.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: OBR scoring structurally penalizes supply-side tax cuts, biasing UK policy toward higher corporate taxes and weighing on UK investment.
insights.quote: you should be looking at that type of policy over a 10 or 20 year time horizon, not a 5year time horizon

insights.claim: Truss says a reported 100,000 shortfall in migration versus forecast was scored as costing 7 billion pounds of headroom, despite migration not generating expected economic returns and adding benefit and public service costs.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: UK fiscal forecasts hinge on migration assumptions; lower net migration mechanically forces tax rises or spending cuts in OBR scoring.

insights.claim: Truss describes a revolving circle between the Treasury, Bank of England, OBR, IMF, Institute for Fiscal Studies and Resolution Foundation that share one progressive Keynesian orthodoxy, with ministers largely barred from using outside experts for official material.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Expect consensus UK economic forecasts to move together; dissenting monetarist views (economists such as those she names at Buckingham University, Patrick Mimford) are underweighted.

insights.claim: Truss says the Treasury is strongly opposed to devolving tax powers to local authorities and is anti-self-employment because it cannot deduct tax at source.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Expect continued tax-collection centralization and pressure on self-employed and contractor structures in UK policy.

insights.claim: McCormack says his town Bedford is essentially broke, statutory requirements have grown faster than revenue, and it received a 50 million pound central government bailout, leaving the council as an administrator of statutory obligations.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack
insights.so_what: Local authority insolvencies signal further central bailouts and local tax rises; relevant to UK municipal credit and services.

insights.claim: Truss expects the next UK general election in 2029 and worries most about Labour winning again in coalition with the Liberal Democrats and Greens, because the right is split between Conservatives, Reform and the insurgent Restore.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: A fragmented right raises odds of continued Labour fiscal policy, wealth taxes and EU realignment through the early 2030s.

insights.claim: Truss believes Andy Burnham, pursuing closer EU relations, has peaked in the polls and that things will get worse for the current Labour government.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Watch Labour leadership dynamics; a Burnham-led push for EU re-entry would affect sterling and trade-exposed UK equities.
insights.quote: I think Burnham has peaked in the polls now

insights.claim: Truss argues meaningful UK reform requires about 350 MPs pledged in advance to vote against new spending and to cut it, since Parliament is sovereign and could abolish the roughly 440 independent public bodies quickly.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Without such a disciplined bloc, expect no structural spending cuts; deficit persistence is the base case.

insights.claim: Truss says Trump moved the Overton window on issues like abolishing USAID and the Department of Education, helped by Tea Party and MAGA grassroots pressure, which Britain lacks.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: A UK populist movement could emerge as conditions worsen, shifting policy rapidly; a regime-change risk for UK assets.

insights.claim: Truss argues that, as in Argentina under Milei, things may have to get really bad, after decades of high inflation, before the public accepts radical reform.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Implies the UK may need a crisis (gilt or sterling) before reform; positions for volatility rather than quick fixes.
insights.quote: it took decades of high inflation and hyperinflation to get a melee

themes.theme: Institutional capture: media, EU and central banks

insights.claim: Truss claims Axel Springer's takeover of the Telegraph and the exit of Allison Pearson and Liam Halligan are a deliberate effort by a pro-EU organization to reduce the conservative media footprint.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Signals migration of conservative audiences to independent media, benefiting creator-led platforms.

insights.claim: Truss argues the push by Donald Tusk's government to gain control of the Polish central bank aims to bring Poland into the euro so it can be controlled, citing Italy under Meloni being constrained by ECB membership.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: Watch National Bank of Poland governance and euro-adoption rhetoric as a driver of zloty and Polish bond risk.
insights.quote: they are trying to get control of the Polish central bank

themes.theme: Bitcoin as a check on state power

insights.claim: Truss says she became interested in Bitcoin in 2017 on joining the Treasury because officials were resistant to it, concluding it challenges their power and can act as a bulwark against centralized power; it features significantly in her book Bank Job.
insights.speaker: Liz Truss
insights.so_what: A former UK prime minister framing Bitcoin as a check on fiat money printing signals growing right-of-centre political support for Bitcoin in the UK.
insights.quote: the minute Treasury officials were resistant to something, I thought it obviously sounded like a good idea
